title: Expert reports in patent litigation: a practical guide
summary: Plan and review a patent litigation expert report with clear opinions, traceable evidence, tested assumptions, useful exhibits, and Rule 26 guardrails.
body_markdown:
*What a retained expert's report needs to make clear, and how patent teams can review the opinions, evidence, and downstream risks before service.*


An expert report in a patent case is the retained expert's signed, case-specific disclosure of opinions and the facts or data, reasoning, and exhibits behind them. It is distinct from attorney argument, the underlying evidence, and the testimony that may follow. The relevant federal baseline is Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(a)(2)(B), and the practical aim is to make each opinion traceable and reviewable.


**Scope note:** This is general information about U.S. federal patent litigation, not legal advice. The assigned judge's scheduling order, local rules, local patent rules, protective order, discovery protocol, and the forum's discovery-sanctions law can change the analysis. Litigation counsel and the retained expert make and own the final professional judgments.


## Key takeaways


- Classify the witness before planning the disclosure. Disclosure requirements depend on the witness's role.
- Connect each opinion to the applicable framework, evidence, method, assumptions, reasoning, and source locator.
- Keep the report case-specific and expert-owned. Counsel may assist, but the witness must prepare, understand, adopt, and sign a Rule 26(a)(2)(B) report.
- Treat disclosure, discovery consequences, and admissibility as separate gates. Satisfying one does not decide the others.


## What is a patent litigation expert report?


A patent litigation expert report makes a reporting expert's anticipated opinions and their bases reviewable before testimony. The first question is which expert-disclosure category applies.


[Rule 26(a)(2)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf#page=59) requires disclosure of any witness a party may use at trial to present expert evidence. A retained or specially employed expert, or an employee whose duties regularly involve giving expert testimony, generally provides the written report described in Rule 26(a)(2)(B). Unless the parties stipulate or the court orders otherwise, the party must provide the narrower subject-matter and facts-and-opinions disclosure under Rule 26(a)(2)(C) for a witness who is not required to provide a report. The latter is a different disclosure, not a deficient report.


A Rule 26(a)(2)(B) report must contain all opinions and their bases and reasons, the facts or data considered, and any exhibits that will summarize or support the opinions. It must also state the witness's qualifications, including all publications authored in the previous 10 years; list all other cases in which, during the previous four years, the witness testified as an expert at trial or by deposition; and state the compensation for the study and testimony in the case.


*Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2)(B), official U.S. Courts text (accessed September 25, 2026).*


Labels alone do not resolve hybrid roles involving employees, inventors, or witnesses with both percipient and specialized knowledge. Counsel should classify the witness from the actual role, anticipated testimony, governing order, and controlling law. This category distinction matters even when the work at hand centers on a Rule 26(a)(2)(B) report.


## Make the opinion path reviewable


A useful report lets a reader follow an opinion from proposition to support without reconstructing the analysis. For every opinion, the report should make six points identifiable:


- the conclusion the expert expects to offer;
- the legal or technical framework the expert was asked to apply;
- the facts, data, documents, testing, or other material considered;
- the method and material assumptions;
- the reasoning from that foundation to the conclusion; and
- the exhibit, calculation, or source locator that lets another reader inspect the support.


These parts can appear in different orders. The quality control is the connection among them, not a preferred set of headings.


Rule 26 distinguishes the facts or data the expert considered from exhibits used to summarize or support an opinion. A materials record should identify actual sources with useful locators, rather than a generic production range or a broad reference to the case file. The[2010 Committee Note](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title28/html/USCODE-2024-title28-app-federalru-dup1.htm) explains that “considered” reaches factual material beyond what the expert ultimately relied upon. A source log, calculation schedule, and stable exhibit references make that record easier to reconcile before service.


Assumptions need the same discipline. Identify the material premise, its source, why the analysis uses it, and whether changing it would alter the conclusion.[Rule 26(b)(4)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf#page=62) protects draft reports and defined attorney-expert communications as work product, but it does not create blanket privilege. Its exceptions address compensation, attorney-provided facts or data the expert considered, and attorney-provided assumptions the expert relied upon.


Counsel may help organize the process, supply the applicable legal framework, test clarity, and review consistency. The witness must still own the substance. The[1993 Committee Note](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCODE-2024-title28/html/USCODE-2024-title28-app-federalru-dup1.htm) recognizes counsel's assistance while requiring a report that reflects the witness's expected testimony and bears the witness's signature.


## Apply that path to the patent opinion at issue


The opinion path changes with the assignment. Technical infringement, validity, and damages work raise different questions and often require different experts. These three opinion lanes are review prompts for the retained expert and counsel, not modules of a universal report.


### Technical infringement and non-infringement opinions


A technical report should connect the operative claim construction, each asserted limitation or asserted equivalent, the accused feature, and the evidence said to establish how that feature works. Product names alone are too coarse. The report should identify relevant versions, configurations, code or documentation, tests, testimony, and pinpoint source locations where those distinctions matter.


Claim construction remains the court's responsibility under[Markman v. Westview Instruments](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/517bv.pdf) . Expert evidence may help the court understand technical usage or resolve subsidiary factual disputes involving extrinsic evidence, as[Teva v. Sandoz](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/574bv.pdf) explains. The expert should apply the operative construction and stay within the assigned technical field. The[Sundance decision](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/08-1068.pdf) reinforces that expert testimony should not instruct the jury on applicable law, a function reserved for the court.


A claim chart can organize the mapping and serve as a supporting exhibit. It does not prove its own conclusion. The narrative must explain why the cited material shows, or fails to show, the claimed feature and how competing technical evidence affects the opinion. That distinction is equally important in a[software patent infringement analysis](https://www.tryandai.com/blog/software-patent-infringement) , where product version and configuration can control the analysis.


### Validity, invalidity, and secondary considerations


A validity analysis should define the relevant person of ordinary skill in the art and relevant date, then tie each material conclusion to the record viewed from that perspective. For anticipation, the report should identify where the cited reference is said to disclose the limitation and provide a source locator that can be checked.


For obviousness, identifying references is only the start. The report should explain the reasoned basis for the proposed combination or modification and address the technical evidence that bears on that reasoning.[KSR v. Teleflex](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep550/usrep550398/usrep550398.pdf) requires an explicit analysis with a rational underpinning, while allowing the reasoning to account for ordinary creativity and inferences available to the skilled artisan.


Secondary-considerations opinions need an equally specific evidentiary path. The report should identify the asserted evidence, the claimed invention to which it is tied, and the basis for any nexus conclusion.[Fox Factory v. SRAM](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/18-2024.opinion.12-18-2019.pdf) shows why unclaimed features and coextensiveness can matter to that case-specific inquiry.


### Damages opinions need their own record and method


Damages is a specialist lane. A report should identify the relevant hypothetical-negotiation date, accused sales footprint, financial data, comparable agreements, royalty form, economic assumptions, and path from the patented contribution to the proposed measure. Each input should reconcile to a source, and each calculation should be reproducible from the disclosed schedules.


[Section 284](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&num=0&req=granuleid%3AUSC-prelim-title35-section284) supplies the statutory floor of a reasonable royalty, but it does not supply a case-specific rate. The report must explain comparability and apportionment rather than treating a license, total product revenue, or the smallest salable unit as a shortcut.[VirnetX 's apportionment holding](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/13-1489.opinion.9-12-2014.1.pdf) explains that identifying the smallest salable unit is only a step toward apportionment when the unit includes unpatented features.[Exmark v. Briggs & Stratton](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/16-2197.opinion.1-10-2018.1.pdf) ties a reasonable royalty to the incremental value of the patented improvement. The en banc[EcoFactor v. Google decision](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/23-1101.OPINION.5-21-2025_2518737.pdf) illustrates the separate need for sufficient facts or data to support a damages expert's premise.


## Use a pre-service quality-control pass, not a universal template


There is no federal form that fits every patent expert, opinion type, or court. Before service, you should test the report against the expert's actual assignment and the case record. Useful questions include:


- Is the witness category confirmed under the governing rules and order?
- Does each opinion state its basis and reasoning, with identifiable evidence and pinpoint support?
- Are considered materials, assumptions, calculations, and supporting exhibits complete, traceable, and internally consistent?
- Does the analysis use the operative claim construction, contentions, relevant dates, and other controlling case inputs?
- Has the expert personally reviewed the final report, resolved drafting artifacts, adopted every opinion, and signed it?
- Has counsel checked the service package against the schedule, local practice, protective order, and court-specific requirements?


Run the checks across the report and every appendix. Recalculate schedules from source data. Confirm quotations and record citations in context. Reconcile defined terms, patent and claim identifiers, product versions, exhibit labels, and cross-references. Look for rationale that exists only in a spreadsheet, an attorney comment, or the team's memory.


These questions are an issue-spotting aid. They do not replace the complete disclosure requirements, the court's order, or case-specific legal advice. Late disclosure can carry consequences independent of the opinion's merits. In[MLC Intellectual Property v. Micron](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/20-1413.opinion.8-26-2021_1825247.pdf) , the Federal Circuit affirmed rulings that separately addressed undisclosed damages material and the reliability of the damages analysis.


## A report begins a later-stage record; it does not end the analysis


Service moves the report into a sequence of later events. Keeping the gates separate helps the team avoid asking the report to do work that belongs elsewhere.


1. **Rebuttal.** A disclosure intended solely to contradict or rebut evidence on the same subject matter has a default 30-day deadline after the other party's disclosure, absent a stipulation or different court order.[Rule 26(a)(2)(D)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf#page=59) supplies that default, while the scheduling order controls the live matter.
2. **Deposition.** An expert who has been identified and whose opinions may be presented at trial may be deposed under the[Rule 26 expert-deposition provision](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf#page=62) . If Rule 26(a)(2)(B) requires a report, the deposition may occur only after the report is provided. The report should permit meaningful examination of the disclosed opinions, but deposition preparation and examination strategy are separate tasks.
3. **Supplementation.** The[Rule 26(e) supplementation duty](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf#page=64) addresses materially incomplete or incorrect information that was not otherwise made known, and it extends to a reporting expert's report and deposition testimony. It is not a reset button for an improved late rationale, method, or theory.[Kemin 's later-evidence record](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/05-1479.pdf) illustrates the contrast: the supplemental analysis followed genuinely new inspection evidence, was disclosed promptly, and met the court's deadline. Whether later-developed material is a proper correction, actual new information, or a change requiring relief depends on the record and governing order.
4. **Admissibility and disclosure consequences.** A complete report does not establish admissibility. The proponent still bears the[Rule 702](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-evidence.pdf#page=30) burden: demonstrate to the court that it is more likely than not that the testimony meets the requirements for helpfulness, sufficient facts or data, reliable methods, and reliable application. The witness must also be qualified for the opinions offered. Separately,[Rule 37(c)(1)](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf#page=82) can limit use of information or a witness that was not properly disclosed, subject to its stated standards.


A complete report makes later scrutiny possible. It cannot guarantee that the opinion will be admitted, credited, or successful.


## Build the report around the case, then have the right people own it


A strong patent expert report reflects the witness's role, the opinion type, the actual evidence, the court's orders, and the applicable law. Its structure should make the reasoning easy to test without turning the document into counsel's brief. The expert owns the opinions and testimony. Counsel owns the legal and procedural judgments. Both should review the final package against the live record before service.
